Gained: both shared contracts R-7 committed this feature to editing are handed back, and the requirement at research/CONVERGE.md:46, that agents resume on their own after a reset, is kept rather than traded away.

Round R-10

R-10 · human — A spawned agent never spawns. It runs helper work inline on every harness, so depth is two everywhere and the third level of the cap is left unused. The guardian is that a spawned agent's brief never grants depth.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 10 answer to L5-13: inline-everywhere. This states the nesting position that PRD.md:129 requires the design to state rather than assume. It takes the capability contract's declared degradation as the rule instead of treating one harness as the degraded case, and it agrees with the harness-agnostic steer upheld at cost in round 7. The price is recorded rather than dressed up: a role with long helper work is slower on the harness that could have run helpers in parallel. Starting a team agent was never in scope for this card and remains refused to every spawned agent under AC-009; nested team patterns stay parked as issue 25.

Round R-9

R-9 · human — Run: all the work done on one feature or bug under a team topology, from the first agent started to the cleanup that kills the last one. Scoped to the feature, sharing a single worktree, outliving any one contact session, which is why a later session adopts it rather than starting a second.

What settled it
Evidence
Grounded in PRD.md:70-77, criteria AC-008, AC-012 and AC-015, and in the round one settled decision that a run outlives its contact session. Defining it by the session instead would have contradicted that ruling. Round 9 answer: accept, with no note and no rewording. Verified by the human under the ratify-here ruling of round 8, so it is a human call rather than an agent coinage. Owed onward to the glossary steward, which is the only writer of the vocabulary file; until it lands there this definition is settled but not yet installed.

R-9 · human — Role: a named position in a team pattern, carrying its own model and lifespan, that one agent fills at a time. The role is the position; the agent is who is standing in it. A role no available transport and model can fill makes the pattern refuse to start.

What settled it
Evidence
Grounded in PRD.md:67 criterion AC-005, PRD.md:74 criterion AC-012, PRD.md:86 criterion AC-024, and the existing vocabulary entry for lifespan. The separation of position from occupant is what the checkpoint rule depends on: a replacement agent reads the checkpoint of the role, not of the dead agent. Collapsing the two would have made that rule unsayable. Round 9 answer: accept, with no note and no rewording. Verified by the human under the ratify-here ruling of round 8, so it is a human call rather than an agent coinage. Owed onward to the glossary steward, which is the only writer of the vocabulary file; until it lands there this definition is settled but not yet installed.

R-9 · human — Spawned agent: any agent the contact agent started to fill a role in a pattern. Never the agent the human talks to. It works from a written brief rather than the conversation, may commit and push its own branch, and is refused every outward action reserved to the contact agent.

What settled it
Evidence
Grounded in PRD.md:42 the agent-class row AC-S, PRD.md:72-73 criteria AC-010 and AC-011, and PRD.md:87 criterion AC-025. The definition names the permission boundary rather than only the parentage, because the access policy already treats the class as carrying its own refusals. Round 9 answer: accept, with no note and no rewording. Verified by the human under the ratify-here ruling of round 8, so it is a human call rather than an agent coinage. Owed onward to the glossary steward, which is the only writer of the vocabulary file; until it lands there this definition is settled but not yet installed.

R-9 · human — Hub: a role other roles may message directly, so their traffic relays through it instead of through the contact agent. A pattern may name one. A hub that is not the contact agent holds no extra authority: it may not start or stop an agent, and it carries a spawned agent's permissions.

What settled it
Evidence
Grounded in PRD.md:43 the agent-class row AC-B, PRD.md:99 the start-or-stop policy row, the round five settled decision that a pattern may name a non-contact hub role, and the existing vocabulary entry for talk edges. The definition separates being a relay point from being in charge, which is what the access policy already says in table form. Round 9 answer: accept, with no note and no rewording. Verified by the human under the ratify-here ruling of round 8, so it is a human call rather than an agent coinage. Owed onward to the glossary steward, which is the only writer of the vocabulary file; until it lands there this definition is settled but not yet installed.

R-9 · human — Stage: one step of the workflow chain, such as designing, planning or reviewing, taken as a unit. It is what the topology map is keyed by, so a stage may have a pattern or none, and it is the boundary the knowledge store's read rules use, where reading a peer within a stage is stricter than reading an earlier stage.

What settled it
Evidence
Grounded in PRD.md:79 criterion AC-017, PRD.md:19, and the round one settled decision that a stage learns its pattern from one central map. Named as an existing workflow step rather than something this feature introduces, which is the honest description: the map gives an existing step a pattern, it does not create the step. Round 9 answer: accept, with no note and no rewording. Verified by the human under the ratify-here ruling of round 8, so it is a human call rather than an agent coinage. Owed onward to the glossary steward, which is the only writer of the vocabulary file; until it lands there this definition is settled but not yet installed.

Round R-8

R-8 · human — The five domain terms with no glossary entry are settled by proposal and human verification on a card, then written by the glossary steward.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-1: ratify-here. The terms are run, role, spawned agent, hub and stage. Their absence was checked directly against the glossary file rather than taken from a digest. The card said plainly that this option is the agent's reading of the rule rather than its letter, because the rule names the requirements interview as the home for a language gap, and the choice was made with that flag visible. Under this option the agent coins nothing unilaterally and the glossary stays another skill's artifact to write. The definitions are owed to round 9.

R-8 · human — The agent lifecycle gets a written table of legal transitions, and the writer refuses a move that is not on it.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-2: edge-table, taken against a precedent count of six to one. The single precedent is the closest relative and its table was read directly rather than summarized: ten states, an explicit allowed-next column, forks and a loop-back rather than a chain, one terminal state, and two invariants each with a named guard. The condition written into the option binds and is not softened here: the table ships with the writer that enforces it, because a table nothing reads is decoration. The table itself is owed to the signature packet.

R-8 · human — Only the contact agent writes the run manifest. An agent that needs an entry asks it.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-3: contact-agent-writes, chosen over the agent's recommendation of splitting the write so an agent could append its own background processes. Recorded as given. The agent's objection was that a self-started background process leaves a window in which it exists and the manifest does not know it. That objection has since been re-checked and it corrects the agent: AC-014 kills an unregistered background process when its owning agent's process tree closes, so the kill is covered and the objection as phrased was too strong. What survives is narrower and is kept because it is real: such a process is invisible to AC-013, which reports only on processes the manifest names, and to the AC-029 dashboard, for the interval before it is reported upward. The ruling also matches AC-009, where only the contact agent starts or stops a team agent.

R-8 · human — The knowledge store's two rules are both guarded on the reading side. An entry is created unfinished, only the authoring agent's clean exit marks it finished, every read filters on finished, and nothing repairs an entry left unfinished by a crash.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-4: accept. There is no writer-side guard because the event that would trigger one is an agent dying, and a dying agent runs nothing. Rejected: a sweep marking orphaned entries, which nothing in the requirements asks for and whose only reader would be a human reading a file that is deleted at cleanup anyway. Cite PRD.md:78-79, criteria AC-016 and AC-017.

R-8 · human — Two aggregates. The run, rooted on the manifest file, owns agent entries, background process entries and each role's running checkpoint. The knowledge store, rooted on the store, owns entries.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-5: accept. Values rather than entities: a talk edge, a team pattern with its roles and models and lifespans, a lifespan, a model name and a role name. Entities: an agent entry, a background process entry and a knowledge-store entry. Rejected: one aggregate over both, because shared deletion is not shared invariants and the finished rule has no bearing on whether a process is alive; and the running checkpoint as its own aggregate, because it exists to describe one agent entry and is deleted with the run anyway.

R-8 · human — This feature raises no domain events. State changes are file writes, and the one asynchronous signal is the waiter's exit.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-6: accept. There is no event mechanism anywhere in the requirements and none was asked for. The reasoning is the rule this design has now applied four times: naming an event with no subscriber is a mechanism with no reader. If a subscriber appears later the events can be named then, against a real consumer.

R-8 · human — The transport adapter family inherits the four existing normalized answer shapes and their exit codes unchanged. No transport vocabulary crosses the boundary.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-7: accept. This is the anti-corruption layer the layer asks for, and it was already the reason an earlier round made transport a fifth adapter family rather than a switch. A pane identifier, a terminal identifier and a subagent handle all arrive in the same shape, and nothing above the boundary learns which transport it is talking to. Cite ADAPTERS.md:27-38.

Round R-7

R-7 · human — The waiter is built and the capability is declared, with a conformance probe for each supported harness. Where the probe fails, the design degrades to the contact agent checking on its next turn and says so.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 7 answer to L4-10: declare-it, with no note attached. This resolves the steer conflict surfaced in the same round in favour of the written rule, which requires capability needs to be declared. The price the human accepted is stated on the card and is not softened here: this feature now edits two shared contracts it does not own, the capability table and the conformance ledger, which is real scope growth for a resumption nicety. What it buys is that a parked agent failing to wake on another harness is reported rather than silent. L4 closes with this card.

Round R-6

R-6 · human — HL-3 Authorization and data scoping is signed: every protected surface with its permitted and denied roles and what actually enforces each, the scoping mechanism for both records, and the three rules nothing can enforce.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 6 answer to HL3-1: sign, with no note attached, so the quote is the mark itself. No approving sentence was written and none is invented here. The packet stated plainly that six of the nine surface rows are enforced by nothing, so a violation is first noticed by a human reading a diff, and that one row is unenforceable in principle because a file read is invisible to hooks and no mechanism could be built for it without a new harness capability. Signing accepted those five risks. The two strongest controls in the table are not this plugin's: merge is guarded by the forge, and the pre-commit gate refuses an agent commit while letting a human through.

R-6 · human — A parked agent is resumed automatically. A background waiter is armed at park time and its exit wakes the contact agent.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 6 answer to L4-9: waker-undeclared, chosen over the agent's recommendation and over the agent's stated strongest objection. Recorded as given. The mechanism is real and documented: DELEGATION.md:34 states that only completion re-invokes a waiting orchestrator, and hooks/stall-watchdog.sh:2-6 states that its exit is the wake-up. What the human accepted with this option is that the capability behind it is undeclared: CAPABILITIES.md:5-22 lists sixteen capabilities and names no background, notification or resumption capability, and providers/CONFORMANCE.md:13-34 carries no probe for it on either harness. The agent surfaced one further consequence in round 7 rather than acting on it: this choice contradicts a written rule in the repository's own steering file, which requires capability needs to be declared. Whether the waiter is declared or not is settled by that card, and every option there still builds this waiter.

Round R-5

R-5 · human — The access policy keeps every row and gains a column naming what actually enforces it. Most rows read convention. Nothing new is built to enforce agent identity.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-1: label-each-row. Taken against a verified finding that no agent identity reaches any hook, that a file read cannot be observed at all because the read tool is outside the shared matcher set, and that every single-writer rule in this plugin is prose with no enforcing script. The ruling keeps design intent on the record where a reviewer can check against it, and refuses to let the document imply a guard that does not exist. The rejected alternatives were narrowing the policy to what a binary agent-or-human signal can enforce, and building the first role-keyed runtime check this plugin has ever had.

R-5 · human — Who resumes a parked agent was re-asked as L4-9 in round 6 and settled in round 11 as S-38: the background waiter is dropped, and the contact agent resumes a parked agent when it next checks the manifest.

What settled it
Evidence
Asked in round 5 and answered with a write-in asking for an argument, which is not a choice, so the card stayed open and L4-9 re-asked it. Round 6 chose an automatic waiter, round 7 declared it as a capability, and round 11 reversed to contact-checks once the waiter was shown to die with the session that armed it. This card sat under still-open on the page until round 21, although S-38 had answered it; it is closed here so the page stops showing a settled question as open.

R-5 · human — A run reports through the existing reporting protocol, unchanged.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-3: accept. A second reporting style would be a second home for the rule and the two would drift. The weighed alternative, a purpose-built format for a team of agents, lost on that ground.

R-5 · human — Each transport verb declares its own time budget and whether repeating it is safe. Nothing retries automatically.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-4: accept. This was already inside the HL-2 signature from round 2, so the row confirmed rather than decided. The weighed alternative, one central retry policy applied by the dispatcher, lost because repeating a verb that starts a process starts a second process.

R-5 · human — No transport verb carries an idempotency key.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-5: accept. An idempotency key exists to make a repeat safe and nothing here repeats without a caller deciding to, so keys would be machinery with no trigger. Consistent with the house answer: zero declarations of idempotency, timeout or retry across the adapter families. The weighed alternative, a key on the start verb, lost because it needs a second store to remember keys while the manifest already records what is running.

R-5 · human — The feature handles no secret. It names models and transports in configuration and never reads, stores or passes a credential.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-6: accept. Credentials already have a home and an owner in this plugin. The weighed alternative, a per-role credential so cheap roles could use a cheaper account, lost because it would put secrets into a manifest that is written to disk and read by a dashboard.

R-5 · human — The topology map is the switch. A stage with no entry in it runs exactly as it does today.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-7: accept. The map that already decides the pattern per stage can say no pattern, so a separate flag would be a second source of truth to keep in step. The weighed alternative, one global switch for the whole feature, lost on that ground while being acknowledged as the blunt instrument you want when something is badly wrong.

R-5 · human — Everything is a short call. Waiting is done by polling the status verb, never by a blocking wait inside a verb.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-8: accept. Already inside the HL-2 signature, and recorded there as the agent's least confident recommendation. The weighed alternative, adding a verb that blocks until an agent finishes, was flagged on the card as voiding the HL-2 signature and re-packeting the verb set; the human did not reopen it.

Round R-4

R-4 · human — HL-1 Persistence is signed: the run manifest file, one agent entry, one knowledge-store entry, and the identity, concurrency, retention and evolution table, exactly as the packet stated them.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 4 answer to HL1-1: sign, with no note attached, so the quote is the mark itself. No approving sentence was written and none is invented here. Signing settled three rows the packet marked as the agent's rather than quoted from a criterion, because the requirements were silent on each: the process identifier, without which AC-013 cannot kill anything it names; a proposed meaning for the word ground, which AC-018 uses once and never defines; and manifest retention, which no criterion states. It also took as accepted the six risks the packet listed. Any later layer that moves a row voids this signature and the packet returns marked with the delta.

R-4 · human — Environment facts are re-detected each run. Nothing about the machine is promoted to any durable register before the knowledge store is deleted.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 4 answer to L3-6: drop-promotion. This removes a clause from AC-019, which is why it was never the agent's to take. It is consistent with the earlier decision that detection reads the session it is in rather than the machine, on the grounds that what is installed and what is usable are different questions. The alternative the human had proposed in round 3, promoting facts into the layered steering file, was weighed on the card and lost on two counts: the fact would be prose an agent reads rather than data a program reads, and every promotion would cost a human approval, so an unattended run could promote nothing.

Round R-3

R-3 · human — The run manifest is keyed by feature alone. The owning contact session is a field inside it, which adoption rewrites.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 3 answer to L3-3: feature-only. This is a ruling on a requirement contradiction, not a design preference. AC-012 keys the manifest by feature identifier and contact session; AC-015 requires a later contact agent to adopt that manifest rather than start a second one. A key holding the old session never matches a new one, so the two could not both hold. The ruling keeps AC-015 whole and edits the key in AC-012, which now reads as an attribute rather than part of the key.

R-3 · human — AC-019's promotion clause is dropped. Environment facts are re-detected each run and nothing about a machine is carried forward.

What settled it
Evidence
Asked in round 3, answered in round 4 as card L3-6: drop-promotion. It stayed open across one round on purpose. The round 3 answer was a write-in naming the repository's layered context harness as the durable register, which contradicted a claim the agent had made. Rather than apply it or dismiss it, the claim was checked and the card re-asked with what the check found. The human was right that the harness is real, layered and stewarded with their own approval on every write. The agent was right that no section shape in it holds a machine fact and that no script reads those files back as data. One part of the write-in was wrong and was corrected on the card: the Codex-side file is not a write target, because no skill writes it.

R-3 · agent — The knowledge store is deleted by the same explicit cleanup step that closes the desktop tool terminals, rather than by a new trigger of its own.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 3 answer to L3-5: accept, audited. The step it rides on already exists for another reason, so this adds an action rather than a trigger. The accepted loss is on the record and unchanged: a session that is killed never reaches the step, so the store survives until the next run for that feature overwrites it.

explicit

explicit

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L1-1: durable-run, no note. This closed session-end teardown as an option before card L2-2 was reached, because a run meant to survive its session must not be ended by the session ending.

What settled it
Evidence
Requirement decision 0007 states that registration alone is not cleanup. A live trial on this machine killed a parent and watched its child and grandchild keep running, so the job object is the guarantee and the manifest is the report. Accepted in round 1.

explicit

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L1-3: accept. Every transport in the catalog starts a local process, a local pane or a local terminal, and none needs a port or a second host.

What settled it
Evidence
The registry check derives families from the adapters directory listing at adapter_registry_check.py:41-46, and the dispatcher builds its path from the family string with no set check at adapter.sh:37-52. Only scripts/afk-config.py and CONFIG.md must change. Accepted in round 1.

explicit

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L2-2: job-is-the-guarantee. The accepted cost is recorded rather than hidden — a killed session kills its agents and leaves nobody to report what could not be killed, which is a known loss against AC-013.

R-1 · human — A stage learns its pattern from one central map held in configuration, keyed by stage name.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L2-3: central-map. The consequence accepted with it is that this feature edits skills it does not own, and the map is the single home for the topology.

What settled it
Evidence

nodes.evidence: > (SDD §5 row "Write repository configuration") | Write repository configuration | Human. One stated exception: the contact agent, through agent-start in the team entry script, copies the git-ignored .claude/settings.local.json of the main checkout into the run's worktree (S-191) | Every agent class, for every other configuration write (S-191) | The one allow rule on the team entry script covers the copy. The script never overwrites: when the file exists, it skips the copy and reports that (S-191). A write into the main checkout: the protected-branch guard refuses an identified mutation of a guarded resource, which is the main checkout on any branch, a linked worktree on a protected branch, or a worktree another live session holds; it judges an edit tool at each target and a shell command at the paths it recognizes as written, while reads, composition and unknown programs pass (hooks/lib/protected_branch_guard.py:7-12, :522-627). So the contact session sits in a linked worktree on an unprotected branch (:572-590), and pane agents of one herdr tab share a worktree as one group, while agents in other tabs need the same AFK_WORKTREE_GROUP (hooks/lib/occupancy.py:32-38). Agents write run-directory files through the team script, never an edit tool or a shell write that names a main-checkout path, which the guard refuses by target; the team script is an unknown program, and the run directory is ignored by git, which the change meter does not watch (hooks/lib/change_meter.py:7), so the manifest stays where S-102 put it (GRILL-LOG.md:745 (7); main-merge delta 2, corrected: a shell write is now refused by target). Every other configuration write: CONVENTION, no gate refuses it | S-191, SET-1, GRILL-LOG.md:745 (7) |

claims.text: the hit set holds every reference to MANIFEST, set_instruction_files over the name forms this pass searched

/afk:setup builds its election at run time from MANIFEST.md: step 2 probes every entry, step 3 offers opt-in rows deselected on every branch from the register (never a hardcoded list), step 4 walks a human: fix through, step 5 re-probes; a declined or no-human opt-in row reports skipped (user choice) with no fix and no re-probe, so a new opt-in row joins with no SKILL.md edit

set_instruction_files.py writes only pluginConfigs."agents-md@builtin".options.instructionFiles into $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json or ~/.claude/settings.json after a .bak backup; H11 runs it, test_set_instruction_files.py pins it and agents-md-config-check.sh reads the value; the planned change edits none of these, so all stay unchanged

The comment gate (first, hooks/precommit-gates.sh:148) and plugin-source-gates.sh's four gates (skill-registry, native-contract, genericity, behavior-registry) run on agent commits only and in CI under the target branch's judge and then the branch's own
Native check A fails a register row naming the harness unless the same commit adds a hooks/native-contract-allow.txt line; PROVIDERS.md and docs/afk are outside check A

Checks G and H key on provider *.sh stems and PROVIDERS.md's Supported harnesses table, so functions added to the existing claude.sh and codex.sh change neither; H (and L under Model tiers) would fail only if a backticked-first-cell table of the new functions were placed in those sections; check K fails any file outside claude.sh, scripts/tests and docs/afk that names a hooks/lib/providers/claude_*.py helper; check J flags a python shebang or python argv in any *.py, not a bash argv

Skill-registry check C reads only hooks/*.sh and hooks/lib/*.sh, so a constant in hooks/lib/providers/claude.sh cannot fail it; a reader of it in those files needs an E-table row. Check E only requires each adapter.json register entry to exist as a heading, so a new row needs no adapter.json entry

The genericity gate blocks ticket-shaped ids (AUTO-1, AUTO-2, INV-068 shapes) in added plugin .md lines outside CHANGELOG.md; the comment gate blocks more than 2 consecutive added comment lines and #N or GH-N in added comments of the new .sh functions and permission.py

No test enumerates provider adapter functions: outside the provider files afk_(claude|codex)_ names appear only at MANIFEST.md:848 and in spec records; hook-smoke.sh loops over adapter files and test_provider_core_dir.py compares provider names with *.sh stems

Register slices pin positions: test_team_transport.py slices C15 to '### C16 ·' and forbids harness names there, so a new row between C15 and C16 breaks it; test_setup_secrets_repo_root.py forbids "no `.afk/config.yaml`" outside H0; a row elsewhere, for example after H14, trips neither

A new scripts/team/permission.py that runs bash -c '. hooks/lib/provider.sh; afk_claude_spawn_allow_rule' through run-hook.py's find_bash follows scripts/team/probe.py and trips no gate or test as long as it carries no python shebang or python argv (J), names no claude_*.py helper (K) and keeps added comments to 2 lines; provider.sh has no dispatcher for the new suffixes, so the script names the function itself

No code in the repository reads or writes a harness permission allow rule or a settings permissions key: permission hits outside docs/afk are the CI token scope, check A's allow-file variable, a file mode, the hook envelope's permission_mode and prose; 'Bash(' appears only as a matcher fixture; the settings readers touch enabledPlugins, claudeMdExcludes and pluginConfigs only
The planned names AFK_SPAWN_ALLOW_RULE, spawn_allow_rule, spawn_rule_files, spawn_rule_lists and permission.py exist only in docs/afk plan records at this head: no code defines or reads them yet

claims.text: Deployment order: the provider functions, permission.py, the register row and the PROVIDERS.md text ship in one plugin tree with no build step, so no side has to ship first; the allow rule itself is added by the human outside the repository

Corrects c-4197ce3c: the comment gate runs only at agent commits (precommit-gates.sh:148, after afk_agent_session at :41); CI never runs it. CI runs pytest over scripts/tests, hook-smoke, and the four plugin-source gates (skill-registry, native-contract, genericity, behavior-registry; plugin-source-gates.sh:97), first under the target branch's runner and then the branch's own. The runner sources its own (judge) provider.sh (plugin-source-gates.sh:193) and points afk_plugin_dir at the candidate tree (:248). At commit time and in the first CI step the judge is the installed copy or the target branch, so the new claude.sh is read only as data. The second CI step (tests.yml:99) runs the branch's own runner, which does source the new adapters

Corrects c-d74fa82f: in check C a reader needs its name mentioned anywhere in MANIFEST.md, not an E-table row: the test is a word match over the whole file (skill-registry-gate.sh:183). Check C builds its assignment set from the same hooks/*.sh + hooks/lib/*.sh universe (:157). So a reader there of AFK_SPAWN_ALLOW_RULE, which is assigned only in hooks/lib/providers/claude.sh, counts as an unassigned external variable

Corrects c-dc429e72: the genericity gate also runs check 0b over the whole plugin tree, tracked and untracked (genericity-gate.sh:135-145). It looks for account ids, addresses and the committer's own handles in every file except LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md and the manifests, so it reaches the new claude.sh, codex.sh and permission.py. Check 0 reads scripts/*.sh only, not recursively (:96), so scripts/team/permission.py is outside it

Refines c-864fc17a: SKILL.md step 3 makes a declined opt-in row skipped (user choice) with no fix and no re-probe (SKILL.md:103-107), and it builds the options from the register (:112-114). The no-human skip is not in SKILL.md: it is written inside the C15 row itself (MANIFEST.md:616-618, pinned by test_team_transport.py:496-498). So the new opt-in row needs its own no-human sentence

pytest runs the gates over the whole tree in CI on both operating systems (tests.yml:64), so any gate finding the change raises also turns pytest red, independent of the plugin-source step. The native-contract gate runs over the committed tree in test_model_tier_gate.py:58 and over a copy of tracked plus untracked files in test_native_contract_events.py:34-59. The registry gate runs in test_skill_registry_gate.py:57, and all four plugin-source gates in test_plugin_source_gates.py:448

provider.sh sources every hooks/lib/providers/*.sh when it loads (provider.sh:13-20), and all 16 files that source it run under set -u, hook-smoke included. So the new constant is evaluated in every hook, gate, create-worktree and plugin-clone run. A literal assignment is safe. An assignment that expands an unset variable, or prints anything, aborts those scripts or turns test_run_hook.py:159-163 red (that test asserts empty stderr). The new constant would be the first top-level statement other than a function in either adapter

Inferred: every adapter is sourced into one shell namespace, claude.sh before codex.sh (provider.sh:13, sorted glob). A provider-specific constant named without the provider (AFK_SPAWN_ALLOW_RULE, not AFK_CLAUDE_...) would be silently overwritten if a later adapter defined the same name. No gate checks for name clashes between adapters

In a pane agent's shell, provider detection answers unknown under the H-2 harness and claude under the H-1 harness. The live record is providers/CONFORMANCE.md:434; the cause is that codex.sh:8 detects only on PLUGIN_ROOT, which only hook processes carry. So permission.py cannot pick the adapter through afk_provider in an H-2 session: it must call afk_claude_spawn_allow_rule or afk_codex_spawn_allow_rule by name, or take the harness as an argument. This supports c-1e0dd929

test_h2_move.py:211-217 reads the text of both claude.sh and codex.sh and asserts that neither contains worktree_folder. It passes as long as the new functions do not mention that key. The first pass could not have found this pin, because it reads the adapter files by path and names none of the subject's simple names

providers/CONFORMANCE.md:402-408 (Add harness, step 2) lists the adapter functions a new harness must define: detect, priority, plugin root, plugin data, managed directory. At head it already omits user_instruction_file, installed_root and enablement, which provider.sh:80 and :118-120 dispatch. A spawn function that both adapters carry also goes unlisted unless that step is updated. No test guards it

The behavior-registry gate also reads PROVIDERS.md and MANIFEST.md. It requires a row labelled Managed behavior, scoped to the nearest header-and-separator above it, whose header carries Claude Code and Codex CLI columns (behavior_registry.py:465-487, 516-524; PROVIDERS.md:34). It also requires MANIFEST.md to keep mentioning afk:behaviors (:500-503). New PROVIDERS.md text that inserts a table header above that row inside Construct mapping fails the gate, and test_behavior_registry.py:696 and test_plugin_source_gates.py:448 pin it. Adding rows elsewhere passes

FRESHNESS.md:76 requires an adapter change to update, in the same commit, the adapter, its helper, its fixtures, the capability and provider columns, the setup section and the conformance row. FRESHNESS.md:73 requires the same for a provider-mapping change. These rows are judged by /afk:setup audit section 4 (AUDIT.md:60), not by a gate. Audit section 2 (AUDIT.md:32) would also list AFK_SPAWN_ALLOW_RULE, named in a skills/ file, as a candidate dependency to check, because it is not an E-table variable

Two more whole-tree tests reach permission.py and the adapters by enumeration, not by name. test_no_review_id_citations.py:26 forbids review ids shaped like A3-004 or CA2-3 in any file outside scripts/tests. Native check J (native-contract-gate.sh:448) refuses a python shebang, a python argv or AFK_PY in any .py file. Check I (:536) refuses CR bytes in any *.sh but not in scripts/team/*.py, and .gitattributes:5 keeps *.sh LF on checkout

hooks/lib/providers/claude.json:29 and codex.json:40 carry an allow list, but it is the protected-branch guard's list of tools that pass through, not a harness permission rule. The H11 writer reads the whole settings object and writes it all back, so a permission rule the human adds survives an H11 run (set_instruction_files.py:49, :92-105). This supports c-51243ddb
